![A. G. Sulzberger during his speech at the WAN-IFRA World News Media Congress. Image from the [Reuters Institute](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/news/new-york-times-publisher-g-sulzberger-why-and-how-news-publishers-should-fight-ai-platforms).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[A. G. Sulzberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._G._Sulzberger), publisher of the [New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/), used the opening remarks at the [WAN-IFRA](https://wan-ifra.org/) World News Media Congress in Marseille to make the news industry's bluntest case yet against the companies leading the AI build-out. The [Reuters Institute](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/) republished the [full text](https://www.nytco.com/press/a-i-journalism-and-the-uncertain-future-of-the-public-square/). The speech was titled "AI, journalism and the uncertain future of the public square," and its thesis is that the profession has been "too quiet, too passive and too fragmented" in the face of AI companies that take journalism without consent or compensation.

The speech's central comparison puts "data" alongside AI's other inputs:

> The first is talent – the people who design the algorithms. The second is what tech companies call "compute." [...] The third is energy [...] The fourth is what tech companies call "data." The word itself seems almost designed to make creative and expressive work sound trivial, a ubiquitous commodity. But "data" is often used, among other things, as a synonym for books, movies, music and journalism – what might more accurately be called "copyrighted content."

What the speech argues:

- **The asymmetry of inputs.** Talent, compute, and energy are all paid for. No lab would ask its best engineers to work free or tap a power line illegally, but "data" is taken without consent or payment, justified by shifting rationales (it's just facts, deals are slow, fair use covers it, national security demands it).
- **The scale gap.** The six leading AI companies are worth a combined $11 trillion and US private AI investment hit ~$350 billion in 2025, yet by the speech's estimate less than half of 1% of that goes to compensate the creators of the training data.
- **The traffic mechanism.** Getting a Google user to click through is [reportedly ten times harder](https://blog.cloudflare.com/content-independence-day-no-ai-crawl-without-compensation/) than a decade ago. Competing AI products send referral traffic at a rate [96% lower](https://web.archive.org/web/20250402222515/https://tollbit.com/bots/24q4/) than Google search. Comscore-tracked newspapers saw average traffic drops above 45% as the AI race intensified, and newspaper advertising revenue is already [down 80%](https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/fact-sheet/newspapers/) over two decades.
- **The reliability problem.** A [European Broadcasting Union](https://www.ebu.ch/) [study](https://www.ebu.ch/files/live/sites/ebu/files/Publications/MIS/open/EBU-MIS-BBC_News_Integrity_in_AI_Assistants_Report_2025.pdf) found leading AI assistants misrepresented the news in nearly half of all answers, and because models express uncertainty poorly they tend to be "confidently wrong," while disclaiming legal responsibility for what they output.
- **Four ways to fight back.**
  - Stand up for your rights: insist that intellectual-property (IP) rights be respected, and push back when they aren't.
  - Deal carefully: weigh each licensing deal's long-term value before signing.
  - Push legislators: reinforce IP protections, require bots to identify themselves, mandate usage transparency, and make AI companies liable for defamatory output.
  - Join together: coordinate across the industry and with other creative sectors.
- **Four ways to stay resilient.**
  - Use AI the right way: set newsroom standards, then put the technology to work.
  - Be a destination: build direct audience relationships instead of relying on intermediated traffic.
  - Focus on original reporting: the work AI can't do and has no other source for.
  - Explain why journalism matters: make the public case that original reporting is essential.

The speech is specific about who: Meta [training on pirated books](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2025/jan/10/mark-zuckerberg-meta-books-ai-models-sarah-silverman), Perplexity [scraping against explicit objection](https://blog.cloudflare.com/perplexity-is-using-stealth-undeclared-crawlers-to-evade-website-no-crawl-directives/), OpenAI [lobbying for legal immunity](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/openai-urges-us-allow-ai-models-train-copyrighted-material-rcna196313), and even Anthropic, "often held up for its commitment to ethical AI development," [declining to pay](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/05/technology/anthropic-settlement-copyright-ai.html) for the journalism it uses. The Times is itself suing [OpenAI and Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Times_Co._v._OpenAI), and later Perplexity, over these practices.

## My Notes

- **The regurgitation charge has outside support**: his strongest legal claim is "substitutive copying, retention and regurgitation" of individual works, and it is testable. A preprint covered in [Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Reactivates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books](/posts/20260501-finetuning-copyright-recall/) found frontier models reproduce copyrighted books word-for-word, and that finetuning reactivates recall traced to pretraining.

- **The cure leans on advice already tried**: "Be a destination" and "direct relationships with audiences" is the go-direct advice of the search/social era, and [more than 3,000 US papers](https://localnewsinitiative.northwestern.edu/projects/state-of-local-news/2024/report/) closed anyway. If AI intermediation is structural, and a 96% lower referral rate suggests it is, that advice may prove too little too late.
